statement: A wrong answer scores 0, like a blank. Kit and Remy get the same 5 questions right. Kit also guesses on 3 more; Remy leaves those blank. Which sentence must be true?

choices.text: Kit always scores more than Remy.
choices.misconception: I thought at least one of the guesses would always be right, so Kit must get more.

choices.text: Remy always scores more than Kit.
choices.misconception: I thought leaving a question blank is safer, so the blanks must give more points.

choices.text: Kit could score less than Remy.
choices.misconception: I thought each wrong guess takes points away, so Kit could fall behind.

choices.text: They always get the same score.
choices.misconception: I thought guesses are only luck, so they never count for any points.

choices.text: Kit never scores less than Remy.

hints: What happens to Kit's score if all 3 guesses are wrong?
Compare the two children question by question. On the 5 shared questions they score the same. On the other 3, a blank scores 0, and a guess scores 0 or more. Then read each sentence carefully.
If every guess is wrong, Kit and Remy tie. If any guess is right, Kit is ahead. Which sentence fits both cases?

solutions.reliable: On the 5 questions they both got right, they score the same. On the other 3 questions, Remy scores 0. Kit scores 0 for a wrong guess and points for a right one, so Kit scores 0 or more there. If all of Kit's guesses are wrong they tie, and otherwise Kit is ahead. So Kit can never score less than Remy, but Kit does not always score more. The idea to keep: when wrong answers cost nothing, a guess can only help, so never leave a blank.

whyOnTest: It states the rule behind never leaving a blank, and the choices separate "never less" from "always more", which students often mix up.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
